summary.text: The tenth substitution iterate has length at most \(4^{10}=1{,}048{,}576\), and every later position is assigned the default symbol \(1\); thus there are too few zero positions, so the defined \(1{,}048{,}578\)-th term falls back to \(1\). Since \(r=(3+\sqrt3)/3\ge 1\), the discrepancy at that index is at least \(1{,}048{,}577>2\), contradicting the proposed bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(0)=01,\qquad \sigma(1)=0100.
\]
The accepted statement represents the word by only a finite substitution iterate, with a default value outside that iterate. We first spell out that construction, since it is the source of the counterexample.

Define finite words \(L_m\) recursively by
\[
L_0=[0],\qquad L_{m+1}=\sigma(L_m),
\]
where applying \(\sigma\) to a word means replacing every letter by its image and concatenating the resulting blocks. More generally, the substitution rule used in the statement sends every natural number other than \(0\) and \(1\) to the empty word, although only the letters \(0\) and \(1\) arise from \(L_0\).

Every substitution block has length at most \(4\): the three relevant cases are
\[
|\sigma(0)|=2,
\qquad |\sigma(1)|=4,
\qquad |\sigma(x)|=0\quad(x\ne0,1).
\]
Consequently, for any finite list \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_t]\),
\[
|\sigma(X)|=\sum_{i=1}^t |\sigma(x_i)|\le 4t=4|X|.
\]
For completeness, this inequality can also be obtained by induction on \(X\): it is immediate for the empty word, and adjoining a first letter adds at most \(4\) to both the relevant upper bound and the substituted length.

It follows by induction on \(m\) that
\[
|L_m|\le 4^m.
\]
Indeed, \(|L_0|=1=4^0\), and if \(|L_m|\le4^m\), then
\[
|L_{m+1}|=|\sigma(L_m)|\le4|L_m|\le4\cdot4^m=4^{m+1}.
\]
In particular,
\[
|L_{10}|\le4^{10}=1{,}048{,}576.
\]

Now define a zero-indexed word-value function \(V\) by reading from \(L_{10}\), but assigning the default value \(1\) whenever the requested index lies outside that finite word:
\[
V(k)=
\begin{cases}
\text{the letter of }L_{10}\text{ at zero-indexed position }k,&k<|L_{10}|,\\
1,&k\ge |L_{10}|.
\end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
P=\{k\in\mathbb N:V(k)=0\}.
\]
We claim that
\[
P\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,1{,}048{,}576\}.
\]
To prove this, suppose that \(k\ge1{,}048{,}577\). Since
\[
|L_{10}|\le1{,}048{,}576<1{,}048{,}577\le k,
\]
the index \(k\) is outside \(L_{10}\). By the definition of \(V\), this gives \(V(k)=1\), so \(k\notin P\). This proves the claimed containment. The containing set has \(1{,}048{,}577\) elements, and therefore
\[
|P|\le1{,}048{,}577.
\]
In particular, \(P\) is finite.

The enumeration operation used to define \(a(n)\) lists the natural numbers satisfying the predicate \(k\in P\) in increasing order, starting with index \(0\). If the requested index is beyond the end of this finite list, its stipulated value is \(0\). Thus, for a finite set \(P\) of cardinality \(c\), requesting its \(j\)-th member with \(j\ge c\) returns \(0\): the valid zero-based indices, if any, are only
\[
0,1,\ldots,c-1.
\]

The sequence in the accepted statement is then defined, using one-based positions, by
\[
a(n)=E(n-1)+1,
\]
where \(E(j)\) denotes the zero-based \(j\)-th element of \(P\), with the just-described default value \(E(j)=0\) if that element does not exist.

Take
\[
n=1{,}048{,}578.
\]
Then
\[
n-1=1{,}048{,}577.
\]
Since \(|P|\le1{,}048{,}577\), the zero-based index \(1{,}048{,}577\) is at least the cardinality of \(P\), and hence lies beyond the last available element of \(P\). Therefore
\[
E(1{,}048{,}577)=0,
\]
and consequently
\[
a(1{,}048{,}578)=0+1=1.
\]

It remains to compare this with the proposed linear approximation. Put
\[
r=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{3}.
\]
Because \(\sqrt3\ge0\),
\[
r=1+\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\ge1.
\]
Using the value of \(a(n)\) just established, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
nr-a(n)
&=1{,}048{,}578\,r-1\\
&\ge1{,}048{,}578\cdot1-1\\
&=1{,}048{,}577.
\end{aligned}
\]
This number is nonnegative, so its absolute value is the number itself; even without using equality, the general inequality \(x\le |x|\) gives
\[
\left|1{,}048{,}578\,r-a(1{,}048{,}578)\right|
=\left|1{,}048{,}578\,r-1\right|
\ge1{,}048{,}577>2.
\]
Thus the asserted bound
\[
\left|nr-a(n)\right|<2
\]
fails at the positive integer \(n=1{,}048{,}578\). Equivalently, the proposed two-sided inequality
\[
-2<nr-a(n)<2
\]
fails there. This supplies the required counterexample to the universal statement.

There is an important mathematical qualification to what has just been disproved. The function \(V\) above is not the genuine infinite fixed point of \(0\mapsto01,\ 1\mapsto0100\): it is the tenth finite iterate followed forever by the artificial default value \(1\). Accordingly, its set of zero positions is finite, whereas the genuine fixed point has infinitely many zeros. The counterexample therefore disproves the accepted statement with its finite-prefix/default-value definition of \(a\). If “A284852” is instead interpreted literally as the zero positions in the genuine infinite fixed point, the step \(a(1{,}048{,}578)=1\) does not apply, and this particular argument is not a disproof of that differently defined sequence.
